technique_name: L12.1.1 Disrupting the Availability of System Services > L12.1.1.1 Loop DoS Attack
description: Loop Dos is used to attack UDP-based user-layer protocols. If both services are defective, for example, when an error message is received as input, both services respond with an error message. If a bad input produces a bad output, and the second system behaves the same, the two systems will send error messages to each other endlessly after receiving the attack trigger, causing the service to be DoSed and the network bandwidth to be exhausted. The attack procedure is as follows:
potential_defenses: Avoid responding to illegal requests and error messages
Increase traffic limits and discard UDP packets under high load
Restrict access to privileged ports (0-1024)
Network segmentation and rate limiting
detection_opportunities: Monitor for abnormal UDP connection spikes via netstat
Detect endless error message loops between services
Use open-source detection scripts (e.g., CISPA loop-DoS verifier)
code_examples_patterns: Craft malformed UDP packets to trigger error-loop between two services
Use scapy or raw socket scripts to send trigger packets to UDP endpoints

technique_name: C12.1.1 Disrupting the Availability of System Services > C12.1.1.1 Destruction of Systems and Data
description: Attackers with the intent to cause disruption may stop or disable services on a system, delete certain core files and data, thereby preventing legitimate users from accessing these services. Stopping critical services may hinder the defender's response to the incident and facilitate the attacker's ultimate objectives.
potential_defenses: Redundant data storage and offline backups
Immutable storage for critical data
Rapid backup restoration procedures
File integrity monitoring
detection_opportunities: Detection of service stop commands and abnormal service termination
Mass file deletion events via file system monitoring
Alerts on critical service unavailability
code_examples_patterns: Execute service stop commands (e.g., systemctl stop, net stop) on critical services
Delete core system files and databases using rm, del, or cipher commands

technique_name: C12.1.1 Disrupting the Availability of System Services > C12.1.1.2 Container Process Connection Attack
description: Containers do not limit the number of process connections. Processes can be created cyclically in containers, which affects host machines, for example, occupying host machine memory and CPU. Docker is used as an example:
potential_defenses: Limit the number of processes within the container
Configure cgroup pids.max limits
Resource quotas and container hardening
detection_opportunities: Monitor rapid process creation within containers
Alert on unbounded PID growth affecting host CPU and memory
Check container PidMode and process limits via docker inspect
code_examples_patterns: Fork bomb to exhaust system resources: () { :; : & }; :
Cyclic process creation within unbounded containers

technique_name: C12.1.1 Disrupting the Availability of System Services > C12.1.1.3 Container Network Storm
description: A large network load is created in the container. As a result, data cannot be transmitted on the host machine network, causing network storms.
potential_defenses: Plan container network with appropriate MTU and QoS parameters
Configure BPS and IOPS restrictions on container networks
Network segmentation and traffic shaping
detection_opportunities: Monitor container BPS and IOPS for anomalous spikes
Detect network storms on host interfaces caused by container traffic
Alert when container network load exceeds configured thresholds
code_examples_patterns: Generate massive I/O load: dd if=/dev/zero of=test.out bs=1M count=800 oflag=direct
Flood container network interface with synthetic traffic

technique_name: C12.2.1 Hardware resource utilization > C12.2.1.1 Hijacking Hardware Resources
description: Attackers intrude through automated scripts, implant mining programs, and other methods to hijack computing resources for profit.
potential_defenses: Monitor abnormal high usage of hardware resources
Restrict outbound connections to known mining pools
Application whitelisting and endpoint protection
detection_opportunities: Monitor for sustained abnormal CPU/GPU utilization
Detect connections to known mining pool domains and IPs
Alert on unauthorized mining processes
code_examples_patterns: Deploy cryptocurrency mining malware (e.g., xmrig, kworker) via automated scripts
Implant mining programs that consume CPU/GPU cycles for profit

technique_name: C12.2.1 Hardware resource utilization > C12.2.1.2 Container Hijacks the Host CPU
description: Containers do not have CPU restrictions. The CPU usage of containers can be continuously occupied, causing the CPU usage of the host machine to increase sharply or even become unavailable. Containerd is used as an example.
potential_defenses: Limit CPU within the container using cpu_shares or CPU quotas
Enforce resource limits via container orchestration policies
Monitor host CPU usage for container-induced spikes
detection_opportunities: Check containers for missing cpu_shares configuration via crictl inspect
Alert when container CPU usage causes host CPU to spike
Monitor for containers running without CPU restrictions
code_examples_patterns: Run CPU-intensive workloads in containers without cpu_shares configured
Use crictl to identify and exploit containers without CPU limits

technique_name: C12.2.1 Hardware resource utilization > C12.2.1.3 Container Hijacking Host Machine Memory
description: Containers do not have memory restrictions. The memory of containers can be occupied continuously, causing the memory of the host machine to increase sharply or even become unavailable. Docker is used as an example:
potential_defenses: Limit memory within the container using Memory cgroup limits
Set docker --memory flags or Kubernetes memory requests/limits
Monitor host memory for container-induced exhaustion
detection_opportunities: Check containers for missing memory limits via docker inspect
Alert when container memory consumption causes host memory spike
Monitor for containers with Memory=0 (unlimited) configuration
code_examples_patterns: Allocate unlimited memory in containers: dd if=/dev/zero count=1048576 bs=4096 > big.csv
Construct scripts to continuously consume container memory without limits

technique_name: C12.2.1 Hardware resource utilization > C12.2.1.4 Container Hijacking Host Machine Disks
description: The container uses the same root directory as the host machine. Big data can be constructed in the container to fully occupy the root directory disk, causing the host machine disk to be fully occupied. Docker is used as an example:
potential_defenses: Restrict container disk mounting to independent directories, not host root
Set disk quotas and storage limits for containers
Use volume mounts with size constraints
detection_opportunities: Check container mount points via docker info and grep Root Dir
Monitor host disk usage for rapid growth from container activity
Alert when container working directory is mounted to host root
code_examples_patterns: Fill host disk from container: dd if=/dev/zero count=1048576 bs=4096 > big.csv
Create large files in containers mounted to host root directory

technique_name: C12.2.1 Hardware resource utilization > C12.2.1.5 Improper Container Isolation Leading to DOS Attack
description: If multiple containers are mounted to the same disk directory, the disk of a single container can be fully written. As a result, the containers mounted to the same disk directory cannot be used. Docker is used as an example.
potential_defenses: Ensure containers use independent disk directories, not shared mounts
Restrict disk mounting and enforce isolation between containers
Set per-container storage quotas
detection_opportunities: Verify containers are not mounted under the same disk directory via docker info
Monitor for disk space exhaustion affecting multiple containers
Alert when dd or similar commands fill shared storage
code_examples_patterns: Fill shared disk from one container: dd if=/dev/zero count=1048576 bs=4096 > big.csv
Exploit shared mount points to deny service to co-located containers

technique_name: C12.2.2 Utilization of Data Resources > C12.2.2.1 Service Data Encryption Ransom
description: Attackers encrypt an enterprise's core data and use it to extort money.
potential_defenses: Redundant data storage and offline backups
Immutable storage for critical data
Rapid backup restoration procedures
Network segmentation to limit lateral spread
detection_opportunities: Detection of mass file modification and rapid encryption operations
Alert on sudden file extension changes across data stores
Monitor for abnormal service behavior during encryption
code_examples_patterns: Recursive file encryption using RSA-AES hybrid scheme on enterprise data stores
Encrypt core service databases and demand ransom for decryption keys

technique_name: C12.3.1 Ingesting Sensitive Messages to Content > C12.3.1.1 Content Ingestion
description: Attackers use the platform to mass-send sensitive messages to users, triggering a political crisis.
potential_defenses: Perform content risk control and verification before delivery
Rate limiting on messaging APIs
Content moderation and filtering pipelines
detection_opportunities: Monitor for mass-sending patterns from single accounts
Detect unusual content volume spikes targeting user populations
Alert on politically sensitive or policy-violating content patterns
code_examples_patterns: Automated mass-messaging scripts to inject sensitive content at scale
API abuse to flood user inboxes with politically sensitive messages
